brief.notification_title: S&P -8.6% week, VIX 36: stay in bills, no semis
brief.market_summary: US stocks just had one of their worst weeks in years. On Friday the S&P 500 fell 3.7% to 6,910, its seventh straight loss and -8.6% for the week. The Nasdaq fell 5.3% and is now negative for 2026, and SMH fell 10.6% as Nvidia dropped 14% on a report of an SEC probe. The VIX closed near 36. Treasuries were the only clean haven: the 10Y fell 12bp to 4.92% and the 2Y 13bp to 4.63%, helped by a drop in UMich 1-year inflation expectations to 3.7%, even though markets still price a December Fed hike at about 99%. Brent settled around $92.6 for a third weekly loss as Hormuz flows return to normal ahead of the 29 Nov OPEC+ meeting. Crypto was liquidated along with stocks: BTC hit a two-year low of roughly $55–57K overnight on $2.3–2.7B of liquidations and $1.25B of weekly ETF outflows, and was back near $59.9K on Saturday.
brief.since_last:
- **Stocks:** Friday's cash session turned a bad week into a rout. S&P -3.7%, Nasdaq -5.28%, Russell -2.76%. SMH -10.6% and XLK -7.3%, while staples rose (XLP +0.67%).
- **Semis:** Nvidia fell 14% to $125.53 on a report of an SEC accounting probe. Broadcom fell 12.2% on a report that Google cut 2027 TPU orders.
- **Treasuries:** Rallied hard. 10Y 4.92% (5.15% a week ago), 5Y -15bp.
- **IEF trigger met:** UMich 1-year inflation expectations came in at 3.7%, against a 4.3% consensus and 4.7% prior. That was the condition for the second IEF tranche.
- **Fed:** Cook warned of larger hikes (n12), and the minutes point to a December increase (n38). Trump again attacked the Fed as "politicized".
- **Gold:** Fell 4.6% to about $3,515 as the dollar held near 19-month highs.
- **Crypto:** BTC made a two-year low overnight, then recovered above $60K before slipping back to about $59.9K.
- **Oil:** Brent posted a third weekly loss, -3.4% to -4% depending on source.
- **Caveats:** US markets are closed until Monday. Several figures conflict across sources: VIX 35.89 vs 37.43, the Brent settle versus the price feed, and Friday's ETF flows.

economic_data.takeaway: A full point lower than the prior reading. This was the trigger for the second IEF tranche. It reduces the case for a 50bp December hike and helped the 1Y-5Y rally of 11-15bp.
Long-run expectations are easing too. That supports Treasuries but doesn't stop a December hike.
In line and still depressed. Current conditions missed (49.4 vs 51.0), so consumers are not a source of upside.

A big miss. New orders were -0.4 and capex fell to 18.9 from 34.9, while prices paid jumped to 58.2 from 43.2. Growth slowing while costs rise is the worst mix for a hiking Fed. The KC Fed composite beat (18 vs 11), so regional data are mixed.
The labour market is loosening slowly, and the rise in continuing claims is the more telling number. This supports the front-end rally.
Adds to the growth-scare evidence the bond market is now pricing.
Real yields near 2.9% set a high bar for equity valuations, especially long-duration tech.

The key print of the week. A 0.4% m/m reading would revive 50bp talk, lift yields and pressure stocks and BTC. A reading of 0.2% or lower would extend the bond rally.
Lands with durable goods, claims and the Beige Book before Thanksgiving, in thin liquidity, so expect outsized moves.

sections.summary: The AI unwind turned into a broad liquidation. The S&P 500 is in correction territory, the Nasdaq is down 10% for the week, and semis had their worst week since 2001 (n78). Good earnings are being sold (Nvidia, Intuit), and the Fed is hiking rather than cushioning the fall, so I'm treating bounces as tradeable rather than a change in trend.
key_points: S&P 6,910.39 (-3.70%, -8.61% week, 7th straight loss). Nasdaq 22,617.73 (-5.28%, negative YTD). Dow -1.93%, Russell -2.76%. VIX 35.89 (37.43 per Investrade).

SMH 400.06 (-10.6% day, -17.8% week). NVDA -14% to $125.53 on an SEC probe report, ~50% below its 6 Oct high, interim CEO after Huang's resignation. AVGO -12.2% on the Google TPU-cut report. MU -13.9%, AMD -13.2%.
Defensives held: XLP +0.67%, XLV -0.12%. The Anthropic IPO priced at $83, traded up to ~$115, then fell back toward issue (n2, n52).
Speculators' Nasdaq 100 net long had already collapsed to 4.3K from 29.1K, so a short-covering bounce is possible. Next tests: HPE Mon, Dell Tue, PCE Wed.

sections.summary: Treasuries rallied as a haven and on softer inflation expectations: 5Y -15bp, 10Y -12bp to 4.92%, 2Y -13bp to 4.63%. December is still priced at about 99% for a 25bp hike, and Cook is warning of more. The curve is pricing a short hiking cycle that the Fed hasn't endorsed, and high-yield credit is starting to crack while investment grade holds.

Fed: ~99% odds of a 25bp December hike. Waller has floated 50bp, Cook warns of larger hikes (n12), and the minutes say higher rates are needed (n38). Trump is attacking the Fed (n61).

sections.summary: Brent settled about $92.57 Friday, a third straight weekly loss, as Hormuz shipments return to near pre-war levels and banks cut forecasts. Daily tanker attacks and Houthi strikes cause short spikes but haven't reversed the trend. OPEC+ sets 2027 policy on 29 Nov.
key_points: Settle: Brent ~$92.57, WTI ~$83.98 (Investrade), with headlines saying oil settled higher on the day (n5). My price feed shows BZ=F at 89.95 (-2.21%), which likely reflects a different contract month, so I'm treating it as unreliable. BNO 59.02 (+0.31% day, -14.35% month).

Bearish drivers: global crude exports at a record (n25), UAE output near a record after leaving OPEC (n169), Morgan Stanley cut forecasts after the US-Iran deal (n171), and Goldman sees a 2027 Brent average of $88 (n87).
Supportive drivers: ~1 Iranian tanker attack a day (UOB), Houthi strikes on Riyadh, Russian refinery runs down ~45% from Ukrainian drones. Citi sees $150 if the Hormuz disruption persists (n173).
Speculative crude net long fell to 63.1K from 74.0K. US oil rigs +6 to 469.

sections.summary: Crypto traded as a high-beta risk asset rather than a hedge. BTC hit a two-year low of roughly $55–57K on $2.3–2.7B of liquidations before bouncing to about $59.9K. ETF outflows were heavy and persistent, and several weaker L1s (SUI, TON, AVAX) are still falling, so I see no evidence of a durable low yet.

BTC ETFs lost $1.25B for the week, including IBIT's record $541M daily outflow on Thursday. Month to date: BTC ETFs -$3.59B, ETH ETFs -$986M. Friday's numbers conflict across sources.

Supply overhang: ETH exchange reserves rose 210K in four days (n67), BTCS warns its $54M Aave loan could be liquidated (n80), and JPMorgan puts BTC mining cost at $86K (n94), which points to miner selling.
Other events: the Chainflip vault drain of $4.86M (n1), a reported Bitcoin node bug, Ethereum's Glamsterdam upgrade possibly slipping to May 2027, and VanEck dropping Gemini as custodian.

brief.instructor_take: What matters most this weekend is that this market is falling with the Fed leaning against it, not toward it. A December hike is about 99% priced, Waller has floated 50bp, and Cook is warning of more. Trump's attacks don't change the committee's math. That's why I give less weight than the crowd does to the "VIX at 36, history says rally" argument (n24): most of those base rates come from episodes where policy was easing. The bond market is telling the more interesting story. The 1-year fell 11bp and the 2-year 13bp on Friday despite a priced hike, which means traders are betting the hikes stop soon because growth is cracking: Philly Fed 6.3 vs 20.6, the leading index -0.3%, continuing claims at 1.76M. What a less experienced eye misses is Philly prices paid jumping to 58.2. Slowing growth with rising input costs is the hardest mix for a central bank, and it's why Wednesday's cluster of core PCE, GDP, durables, claims and the Beige Book, landing in thin pre-holiday trading, matters more than anything Monday. Semis are the epicentre, and their problems are company-specific (an SEC probe, a CEO vacuum, TPU cuts), so they're hard to value and easy to stay out of. My positioning: bills as the core, IEF held at full size, no semis, and at most a small, staged defensive equity position after the data. I could be wrong in the obvious way: a 5-10% short-covering rally is very plausible from here, and I'm accepting that I'll miss the first leg rather than buy a falling AI complex before Dell and PCE.

top_ideas.title: T-bills stay the core while the Fed hikes
top_ideas.one_liner: Fed still hiking: keep T-bills as core and dry powder
top_ideas.thesis: The Fed is priced at about 99% for a December hike, and Waller and Cook are flagging more. Bills pay 4.3–4.4% out to six months with almost no price risk, and their yield resets higher with each hike. SGOV also funds the staged XLV buy and any later semis rebuild.
top_ideas.reasoning: I start from the policy regime. The Fed is tightening into this selloff rather than rescuing it, so cash isn't dead money: the 3-month bill pays 4.32% and the 6-month 4.38% on the par curve, about a point above the 3.2% core PCE expected Wednesday. Friday showed the other half of the case. In a liquidation even gold (-4.6%) and bitcoin failed as hedges, and only Treasuries and the dollar held up. I prefer SGOV to SHY because the 2-year just fell 13bp in a day: SHY has already banked part of the growth-scare rally and would give some back on a hot PCE, while SGOV carries essentially no rate risk. The concept is optionality. Dry powder in bills lets me buy on my terms after Wednesday's data instead of on Monday's open. What would change my mind is the 13-week yield breaking below 4.0%, or Williams on Monday signalling that December is the last hike. At that point the market is pricing cuts, and I'd rather own more IEF than bills. Newer investors miss that sitting in bills feels like doing nothing, but with the VIX at 36 and a hiking Fed it's an active, positive-carry position.

top_ideas.sizing: The core cash sleeve: all undeployed cash; no cap needed

top_ideas.title: No semis through HPE and Dell; beats get sold
top_ideas.one_liner: No semis through HPE and Dell; beats still get sold
top_ideas.thesis: Record results from Nvidia and beats elsewhere were sold. The sector's overhangs (an SEC probe, a CEO vacuum, Google TPU cuts) are unresolved. SMH fell 17.8% this week, but a bounce isn't a change in trend, so stay out until a hardware beat is actually rewarded.
top_ideas.reasoning: My rule last week was no semis until good news gets rewarded, and this week was a clean test. Nvidia posted record $115.8B revenue and guided above, Keysight beat and raised, and Intuit beat by about $0.21. Nvidia still fell 14% Friday and Intuit 12.8%. When beats get sold, the problem is the multiple and positioning, not the quarter. The overhangs are company-specific and open-ended: an SEC civil probe of Nvidia's disclosures, an interim CEO after Huang's resignation, and a reported ~1M-unit cut to Google's 2027 TPU shipments that hit Broadcom 12%. I agree with the cycle point in n20: memory stocks look cheapest on trailing earnings right at peak pricing, so Micron's low P/E is a warning, not a gift. A 10%+ oversold bounce in SMH is very possible, and I accept missing it. Dell's bar is steep at $6.55 against $2.35 a year ago, so the next 48 hours are a real test. If Dell beats and both the stock and SMH rise, and SMH then holds above 445 for two closes, I'll start rebuilding. Until then, not owning it is the cheapest risk control available.

top_ideas.entry: No new semis buying. After Dell reports, if SMH closes above 445 on two straight sessions and Dell rose on its results, buy half the previously trimmed amount from SGOV. Buy the second half after a further week above 445.
top_ideas.invalidation: Two consecutive SMH closes above 445 after a positively received Dell report end the avoid. If SMH breaks below 400 after Dell, extend the avoid into December.
top_ideas.sizing: 0% now; rebuild in two halves of the prior trimmed amount only on the trigger

top_ideas.title: Small staged XLV starter after MDT and PCE
top_ideas.one_liner: Small, staged XLV starter after Medtronic and PCE
top_ideas.thesis: Health care is where money is hiding: XLV -0.12% Friday vs the S&P -3.7%, and -2.2% over a month vs -9.8%. It has little exposure to the AI capex unwind. A small starter in two tranches around Medtronic and PCE adds equity exposure without betting on an index bottom. XLP is the lower-beta alternative.
top_ideas.reasoning: I'm not trying to call the S&P bottom. I want a small, measured equity position in the part of the market that isn't the problem. The evidence is relative strength: XLV barely moved Friday while the index fell 3.7%, and BJ's beat-and-raise plus staples rising tell the same story of money rotating toward steady earnings. Health care earnings don't depend on GPU orders or AI capex, so the semis overhangs don't flow through. I choose XLV over XLP because staples are already up on the month and more crowded, while XLV still has a 6% weekly drawdown to recover. I stage around Medtronic on Tuesday and core PCE on Wednesday because a 0.4% m/m PCE would push yields up and drag everything, defensives included. XLV's -6.15% week shows that correlations converge in a liquidation. A close below 170, about 4% under Friday, would tell me the selling has spread into defensives and this is de-risking, not rotation. Conviction is low and size is small because in a VIX-36 market even a defensive sector can drop a few percent in a session.
catalysts: Mon 23 Nov after close: Agilent (est EPS $1.72)
risks: Broad forced selling drags defensives too (XLV -6.15% this week)

top_ideas.entry: Tranche 1 (0.75%) on Tuesday after Medtronic's pre-market report, if XLV holds above 174. Tranche 2 (0.75%) on Wednesday after PCE, only if core m/m is 0.3% or lower. Fund both from SGOV; skip tranche 2 if PCE is hot.
top_ideas.invalidation: An XLV close below 170, or core PCE at 0.4% m/m or higher along with Fed speakers backing 50bp.

brief.prior_ideas_review:
SGOV (add): Worked as designed. It held value while the S&P fell 3.7% Friday and 8.6% on the week. The 13-week yield is 4.122% (4.147% at the last brief), above the 4.0% invalidation, and a December hike is still ~99% priced. Keep; it's idea #1 again.

IEF (add second half): The trigger fired. UMich 1-year expectations came in at 3.7%, below the 4.3% threshold, so the second half was due after 10:00 ET Friday. The first half from about 90.67 is now 91.65 (+1.1%). I don't have Friday's intraday prices, so a second-half fill would have been somewhere in the afternoon range up to the 91.65 close. Hold the full 2–3% and don't add after a 24bp weekly rally into $183B of supply and a PCE print. Now that the position is full, tighten the invalidation to a 10Y close above 5.20% (IEF about 89.6), from 5.30%. Keep it, but it's not a new idea today.

SMH (avoid): Right call. SMH fell 10.6% Friday to 400.06 and 17.8% on the week, and the $500 re-entry trigger is now 25% away and no longer useful. Keep, with the trigger reset to two closes above 445 after a well-received Dell report. It's idea #2.

lesson.explanation: Normally different assets move on different drivers, which is why diversification works. In a forced-selling phase, leveraged investors facing margin calls sell whatever is liquid or still in profit, not what is most overvalued. So assets that usually diversify, like gold and bitcoin, fall alongside stocks. Correlations converge toward one, and only the assets that serve as ultimate collateral (Treasuries and dollar cash) hold up. The lesson is to judge a hedge by how it behaves when everyone needs cash, not by its label.
lesson.todays_example: Friday: S&P -3.7%, gold -4.6%, silver -7.4%, and BTC to a two-year low with $2.3–2.7B of liquidations (n4, n35). That came despite claims that bitcoin moves against AI stocks (n64). Meanwhile TLT rose 1.37%, IEF 0.91% and SGOV was flat, with the dollar near 19-month highs. Even XLV, the best defensive, fell 6% on the week. Within credit, LQD rose while HYG fell, showing that risky credit trades like equity in a liquidation.
